overview: Language is strongly left-lateralized in most individuals and organized around a perisylvian network. Broca's area (posterior inferior frontal gyrus) supports speech production and syntactic processing; Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus) supports auditory comprehension; and the arcuate fasciculus links the two, mediating repetition. Contemporary dual-stream models (Hickok & Poeppel) divide this network into a dorsal 'how' route (articulatory/phonological mapping) and a ventral 'what' route (sound-to-meaning mapping).

citations.source: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science, 6th ed. (2021), Ch. 55
Purves et al., Principles of Cognitive Neuroscience, 2nd ed. (2013), Ch. 12

function: Pars triangularis (Brodmann area 45), part of Broca's area; involved in semantic retrieval and syntactic processing.
Contributes to speech planning together with the adjacent pars opercularis (BA 44).

clinical.note: Lesions of the inferior frontal gyrus cause effortful, telegraphic speech with relatively preserved comprehension.

function: Pars opercularis (Brodmann area 44), the posterior portion of Broca's area; central to phonological encoding and articulatory planning.
A key node of the dorsal language stream.

clinical.note: Left inferior frontal damage can impair motor speech planning distinct from aphasia.

function: Posterior superior temporal gyrus is the core of Wernicke's area, essential for phonological processing and auditory comprehension.
Contains the planum temporale, a site of leftward asymmetry implicated in language lateralization.

clinical.note: Fluent but paraphasic, often incomprehensible speech with severe comprehension deficit.

function: White-matter tract connecting posterior temporal (Wernicke) to inferior frontal (Broca) cortex.
Mediates repetition and phonological working memory (the 'dorsal route').

clinical.note: Disproportionate impairment of repetition with relatively fluent speech and preserved comprehension.

function: Inferior parietal cortex integrating visual, auditory, and somatosensory information for reading and semantic access.
Central to written-word processing (visual word form → meaning).

clinical.note: Left angular-gyrus lesions produce agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right confusion, and can cause alexia with agraphia.

function: Part of the inferior parietal lobule supporting phonological storage in the verbal working-memory loop.
Contributes to phonological retrieval during naming.

clinical.note: Left supramarginal damage is associated with phonological errors in speech output.

questions.stem: A patient speaks fluently but with frequent paraphasias and markedly impaired comprehension. Where is the most likely lesion?
questions.explanation: Fluent, paraphasic speech with poor comprehension is Wernicke's (sensory) aphasia, classically from posterior superior temporal gyrus damage.

questions.stem: Selective, disproportionate impairment of repetition with preserved comprehension and fluency is termed:
questions.explanation: Conduction aphasia reflects disruption of the arcuate fasciculus connecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas, sparing comprehension and fluency while breaking repetition.

questions.stem: In Hickok & Poeppel's dual-stream model, the dorsal stream primarily supports what function?
questions.explanation: The dorsal stream maps auditory speech signals onto articulatory/motor representations (the 'how'), while the ventral stream maps sound to meaning (the 'what').

questions.stem: Find the frontal area whose lesion causes non-fluent (Broca's) aphasia.
questions.explanation: Broca's area lies in the posterior inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis and opercularis); its damage produces non-fluent aphasia.

questions.stem: Find the white-matter tract whose disconnection impairs repetition (conduction aphasia).
questions.explanation: The arcuate fasciculus links Wernicke's and Broca's areas; its interruption produces conduction aphasia with impaired repetition.
